analytic.title: A Novel Framework for Quality-Aware Resource Management in Phased Array Radar Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper addresses the problem of operating parameter assignment to multiple real-time tasks in a phased array radar system. The objective is to maximize the resulting system utility while ensuring the schedulability of all tasks with the assigned operating parameters. For this, we propose a novel framework by integrating the existing resource management framework called QRAM (QoS-based Resource Allocation Model) with the notion of schedulability envelope. The schedulability envelope designed offline hides the complex details of phased array antenna scheduling and provides a linear formula as its quantitative abstraction. This abstraction allows QRAM to find the optimal resource assignment without concerning the details of complex scheduling. Our experimental results show that the proposed framework can achieve significantly improved system utility compared to the existing techniques.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: QoS research recognizes that the quality or utility of a real-time task depends on its operating parameters. For example, the accuracy of a feedback control task depends on its sampling frequency and control algorithm. In many realtime systems, there are multiple concurrent real-time tasks and also multiple options of operating parameters from which the tasks can choose. Thus, the question to be answered is how to assign operating parameters to tasks such that all tasks are schedulable with the assigned parameters and the total sum of task utility, called system utility is maximized. This problem has been addressed as a resource management problem [13], [12], [8] by interpreting the parameter combination assigned to a task as its utilization (or resource consumption) and comparing the total utilization with the schedulable utilization bound [10] (or the total resource budget).

The goal of this paper is to find the optimal parameter assignment to maximize the system utility in a phased array radar system where multiple tasks for real-time target tracking are concurrently running. A target tracking task periodically measures its target position and executes a tracking algorithm to estimate the new position. The tracking algorithm is executed on the processor resource (RCC-Radar Control Computer and DSP-Digital Signal Processor) and the target position measurement is made by the phased array antenna as illustrated in Figure 1. The task scheduling problem on the processor resource is fairly well studied [3], [7]. More challenging problem is scheduling of measurement requests called radar dwells on the phased array antenna. Depending on the sampling period with which the track algorithm is operating, a periodic sequence of radar dwells is generated for each tracking task as in Figure 1. Each radar dwell consists of three parts: 1) radar beam transmission (illumination), 2) waiting for radar beam reflection from the target, and 3) radar beam reception. The tracking task utility depends on all these parameters: sampling period, radar beam transmission duration Fig. 1. End-to-end model for a radar task and power, and beam reception duration. For example, a higher sampling rate can provides higher accuracy of target tracking. Also, a longer duration of radar beam transmission and/or higher transmission power allow us to extract more accurate target information from the reflected signal. If multiple options are available for sampling period, radar beam transmission duration, power, etc., our problem is how to assign the parameter options to multiple tracking tasks such that the radar system utility can be maximized. The parameter assignment solution should be feasible in the sense of schedulability for each task to gain the promised utility with the assigned parameters.

The problem looks similar to the aforementioned traditional resource management problem. However, the previous techniques based on the utilization bound check are not directly applicable because the classical definition of utilization and utilization bound cannot capture the complex physical nature of phased array antenna scheduling. First, the beam transmission time and reception time of a radar dwell are not preemptive. However, during the wait time, another dwell can be scheduled as long as the time distance between beam transmission and reception is met. This technique called radar dwell interleaving can significantly save the total schedule time of radar dwells [2]. Second, the accumulated beam transmission duration for a given time window should be less than the threshold to prevent overheating of phased-array antenna panel [1], [15], [2]. This is called the transmitter duty cycle (TDC) constraint. Also, the total energy consumption during a given time window should be less than the threshold, which is called the energy constraint. These physical constraints limit the maximal interleaving of radar dwells. The complex physical characteristics of the phased array antenna-interleaving, TDC constraint, and energy constraint, create a challenging scheduling problem to best trade off the interleaving and physical constraints, which renders traditional utilization and utilization bound over-pessimistic or even useless.

To overcome this difficulty, this paper proposes a novel framework by integrating the previous optimal resource management framework called QRAM (QoS-based Resource Allocation Model) [12], [8] with the notion of schedulability envelope. The schedulability envelope is a linear quantitative abstraction of the complex radar dwell scheduling for a simple schedulability check without concerning the complex details of radar dwell scheduling. Thus, QRAM can use the envelope instead of utilization and utilization bound to find the optimal parameter assignment in a phased array radar system. The contribution of this paper is summarized as follows:

• Build a new framework that makes QRAM work with complex radar dwell scheduling in the phased array antenna, and • Develop a scalable way to derive the schedulability envelope that works for a large number of fine-grained parameter options, which is essential to give QRAM more flexibility of parameter selection. The rest of this paper is organized as follows: In the next section, we formulate the problems and describe the overall approach to integrating QRAM with the schedulability envelope. Section III explains a scalable method to derive a schedulability envelope. Section IV presents our experimental results. Finally, Section V concludes this paper.

div.head: II. PROBLEM DESCRIPTION AND OVERALL APPROACH A. Assumptions and Problem Description
div.p: A radar task for target tracking can be modeled as an end-to-end task [4], [16] as shown in Figure 1, whose first subtask is executed on the processing resource (RCC and DSP) and the second subtask is executed on the antenna. The first subtask processes the previous radar return signal, estimates the next target position, and issues a radar dwell command to steer the radar beam to the estimated position. The second subtask steers the radar beam direction, transmits a radar beam to the direction, receives the reflected beam from the direction, and finally gives the received return signal back to the first subtask. All these should be completed within a sampling period, which is the end-to-end deadline. We assume that the end-to-end deadline is divided into two intermediate deadlines for the two subtasks (see Figure 1) using a deadline assignment algorithm [16], [4]. Also, we assume that a nongreedy synchronization protocol [4], [16] is used between the processor and antenna in a way that makes periodic release of radar dwells as shown in Figure 1. Thus, we can regard each subtask as an independent periodic task on each resource. Generally, the processor part is not a bottleneck since the execution time in the processor part is quite small because multiple vector processors and high-end computers are used in most modern radars [7]. On the other hand, the length of a radar dwell cannot be reduced since it is determined by the physical radar beam round-trip delay. Thus, this paper mainly considers the antenna part as the radar resource.

A radar dwell subtask, or simply a task, is denoted by a 3tuple (J, p, d) where J, p, and d are the dwell pattern, sampling period, and relative deadline, respectively. A dwell pattern J is denoted by a 4-tuple (tx, wa, rx, pw) where tx is the radar beam transmitting time -called Transmitter Duty Cycle (TDC), wa is the waiting time, rx is the receiving time, and pw is the beam transmission power 1 . The beam transmission time tx and reception time rx cannot be preempted and the time distance wa between them should be preserved to successfully receive the radar beam reflected from the target. The deadline d is assumed to be equal to the sampling period p for the simplicity of explanation. This assumption can be 1 The power for receiving the reflected radar signal is negligibly small compared to the transmission power. Thus, we consider only transmission power. relaxed for the case of d < p using techniques for dealing with early deadlines [11].

Each task can operate with diverse options for each parameter domain, tx, wa, rx, pw, and p. Let N tx , N wa , N rx , N pw , and N p denote the number of available options in the corresponding domains. By picking up one option from each parameter domain, we can form an operating parameter combination called a setpoint denoted by Q s = (tx s , wa s , rx s , pw s , p s ). The total number of setpoints denoted by K is N tx × N wa × N rx × N pw × N p . We should assign one setpoint to each task to operate it. We use Q si to denote the setpoint assigned to task τ i .

The quality or utility of a task τ i depends on its assigned operating setpoint Q si . We assume that the utility value that task τ i can gain with operating setpoint Q s = (tx s , wa s , rx s , pw s , p s ) is given as V τi (Q s ). The radar experts can give such utility function by combining the objective measure like track error and the subjective measure like target's semantic importance considering mission scenarios. Note that the utility V τi (Q s ) is given based on the assumption that the task is schedulable with the operating setpoint Q s meeting the temporal constraints of dwell pattern (tx s , wa s , rx s ) and deadline d s (= p s ). Otherwise, the task cannot gain the utility value V τi (Q s ).

The utility value varies even for the same setpoint depending on the target states like target range and speed. To handle this dynamics of a target, we can quantize the target range and speed into discrete regions. The task for tracking a target crossing over the region boundaries can be modeled as a sequence of different tasks with different utility functions. As long as the target is within a region, its tracking task and utility function are fixed. Thus, at any time instant, we can assume that the system has a fixed set of tasks denoted by T askSet where each task τ i has a fixed utility function V τi (Q s ).

With these settings, our problem is described as follows: Problem Description: Which setpoint Q si should be assigned to each task τ i ∈ T askSet to maximize the system utility, i.e., the total sum of task utility:
div.formula: Maximize τi∈T askSet V τi (Q si ) (1)
div.p: under the constraint of schedulability of every task τ i with its assigned parameter combination, i.e., setpoint
div.formula: Q si : Subject to ∀τ i ∈ T askSet, τ i is schedulable with operating setpoint Q si . (2
div.p: In the above problem, we naturally encounter the problem of radar dwell scheduling since the schedulability is the constraint when maximizing the system utility. The radar dwell scheduling is challenging due to the complex physical characteristics of phased array antenna. First, the radar beam can be steered very quickly thanks to the electronic phase shift [2]. Thus, during the wait period wa of a radar dwell J = (tx, wa, rx, pw), the radar beam can be steered to another direction to serve another radar dwell J = (tx , wa , rx , pw ) as long as the beam can be steered back to the original direction within wa to receive the beam reflection of the first dwell J. This technique called interleave can significantly save the time for scheduling radar dwells. Figures 2-(b) and (c) compare no-interleaved and interleaved scheduling of three radar dwells J 1 , J 2 , and J 3 in Figure 2-(a). Second, the phased array antenna has physical constraints due to limited capacity of prime power generator and heating of transmitters on the antenna panel [2]. The TDC (Transmitter Duty Cycle) constraint limits the cumulative TDC over the averaging time window A under threshold T DC th , to prevent overheating transmitters. Also, the energy constraint limits the average energy consumption over A under threshold E th to prevent overloading the prime power generator. Note that interleaving radar dwells intensively use TDC and energy for a given time and thus can be a burden to the physical constraints. Considering these physical characteristics, the objective of the radar dwell scheduling problem is to maximally take advantage of interleaving while satisfying the physical constraints.

div.head: B. Overall Approach
div.p: To tackle the above combined optimization problem of setpoint assignment and radar dwell scheduling, our overall approach is to integrate QRAM with the notion of schedulability envelope. Let us first explain how we apply QRAM to our problem. As an input of QRAM, the utility of task τ i is given as a function of setpoint Q s , i.e., V τi (Q s ). This function is called a setpoint-utility relation and Figure 3-(a) shows examples for three tasks. QRAM also assumes that the amount of resource R(Q s ) required by a task operating with setpoint Q s is given (One example is the task utilization R(Q s ) = e s /p s for operating a task with a setpoint Q s = (e s , p s ) where e s is execution time and p s is period). An example of the setpoint-resource relation is given in Figure 3-(b) 2 . Note that the required amount of resource depends on task's operating setpoint but not on the task's target state and thus there is only one setpoint-resource relation. ( 4) is a direct consequence of the original objective in Eq. ( 1) by replacing V τi (Q si ) with V τi (R i ). The new constraint in Eq. ( 5) is the transform of the schedulability check in Eq. ( 2) to the resource bound check, just like utilization bound check for schedulability check. The transformed problem is to find the optimal amount of resource R i assigned to each task τ i ∈ T askSet to maximize the total sum of utility, under the constraint that the total sum of R i cannot be larger than the resource bound R bound . QRAM can quickly find the near optimal solution by traversing the convex-hull frontiers of the resource-utility relations as in Figure 3-(c). More specifically, QRAM first assigns the minimum amount of resource to each task. If there is remaining resource, QRAM assign more resource to a task whose slope from current frontier to next frontier is the highest. The rationale of this is to maximize the utility improvement by unit increase of resource consumption. QRAM repeats this until the total amount of assigned resource reaches the resource bound R bound . In order to make the above optimization process work for our phased array radar problem, the following issues need to be addressed:

• How to quantify the amount of resource R(Q s ) required for a task to operate with setpoint Q s = (tx s , wa s , rx s , pw s , p s )? • How to define the resource bound R bound such that the resource bound check in Eq.( 5) can be used in lieu of schedulability check?

One way to answer these questions is to forgo the physical characteristics of phased array antenna. If we do not consider interleaving of multiple radar dwells, we can conservatively regard each task τ i operating with setpoint Q si = (tx si , wa si , rx si , pw si , p si ) as an independent periodic task with execution time of tx si + wa si + rx si and period of p si . Therefore, the resource amount R(Q si ) is given by the traditional task utilization, i.e., (tx si + wa si + rx si )/p si . The schedulability check of all tasks is now possible by the following utilization bound check τi∈T askSet
div.formula: tx si + wa si + rx si p si ≤ U bound - max(tx + wa + rx) min(p)(6
div.p: ) where min(p) is the minimum period option and max(tx + wa + rx) is the sum of maximum options of tx, wa, and rx. In this check, we conservatively assume that the whole duration of a dwell tx + wa + rx is non-preemptive to simply preserve the time distance wa between tx and rx. Thus, the above inequality is the non-preemptive version of utilization bound check for EDF (Earliest Deadline First) or RM (Rate Monotonic) scheduling where U bound is 1.0 for EDF and 0.69 for RM and max(tx + wa + rx)/ min(p) is the worst case non-preemptive penalty. If we use this inequality for the schedulability check, R bound used in Eq. ( 5) is given by U bound -max(tx + wa + rx)/ min(p).

However, this naive non-interleaved scheduling assumption cannot take advantage of dwell interleaving. This implies that the above quantification of R(Q s ) and R bound is too pessimistic. Therefore, the QRAM solution based on this naive model gives an unnecessarily limited system utility. This is why we need to integrate QRAM with the notion of schedulability envelope that can more accurately quantify R(Q s ) and R bound by taking advantage of interleaved radar dwell scheduling.

The idea of schedulability envelope is to perform the schedulability analysis taking care of complex radar dwell scheduling in the offline phase and abstract the results as a linear formula for an efficient feasibility check (i.e., schedulability check) of a setpoint assignment solution. When the number of setpoints is K, a setpoint assignment solution can be represented as a K-tuple (n 1 , n 2 , • • • , n K ) meaning that n 1 tasks are assigned with setpoint Q 1 , n 2 tasks with setpoint Q 2 and so on. As such, the schedulability envelope enables QRAM to find the optimal resource assignment without concerning the details of radar dwell scheduling.

One way to find the schedulability envelope was proposed in our previous work [9]. However, it is based on the exhaustive exploration of the solution space and hence not scalable to a large number of setpoints that causes the solution space explosion. The number of setpoints K easily goes up to hundreds and thousands if QRAM wants to have flexibility of parameter selection from fine-grained options in tx, wa, rx, pw, and p parameter domains. For example, if we have five options for each of tx, wa, rx, pw, and p domains, i.e., N tx = N wa = N rx = N pw = N p = 5, then the total number of setpoints K is 5×5×5×5×5. Supposing that the maximum number of schedulable tasks with each setpoint is 100, the number of solutions we need to explore is 100 5×5×5×5×5 . In general, the number of solutions we need to explore is O(n K ) where n is the maximum number of schedulable tasks with each setpoint and
div.formula: K = N tx × N wa × N rx × N pw × N p .
div.p: Due to this huge overhead, our previous method fails to derive the schedulability envelope for a large K. Therefore, we need a scalable way to derive a schedulability envelope to make QRAM work for our problem with a large number of parameter options. The next section will describe such a scalable way to derive the schedulability envelope.

div.head: III. RADAR DWELL SCHEDULING AND ENVELOPE
div.p: For offline derivation of schedulability envelope, we have to presume the online scheduling of radar dwells. In the following subsection, we first explain a heuristic online algorithm to schedule radar dwells by taking advantage of interleaving under the physical constraints. Then, Subsection III-B explains the offline phase to derive the schedulability envelope for the presumed online radar dwell scheduling.

div.head: A. Radar dwell scheduling with hierarchical interleaving
div.p: This section describes our online scheduling of radar dwell tasks in T askSet supposing that their operating setpoints have been already determined. We also assume that tasks operating with the same period option are phase-synchronized using the technique in [9]. Since only dwells from phase-synchronized tasks with the same period option can repeatedly be interleaved at every period, we interleave only those dwells. Therefore, the group of tasks using one period option can be independently handled from other groups of tasks using different period options. Based on this, we first explain our scheduling focusing on a group of tasks using the same period option p. Thus, from now on, a setpoint assigned to a task in the same period group is denoted by Q s = (tx s , wa s , rx s , pw s ) excluding the period domain. Hence a complete setpoint including period p is now denoted by Q p s . With these new denotations, a setpoint assignment solution for T askSet is represented by

Once two blocks are interleaved according to a rule, they become a single block as shown in the right most column of the table. The single block is abstracted again with (a,b,c,T,E). For determining the new a, b, and c, we have two choices for each rule as shown in the right-most column of the table. By recursively applying the rules along the hierarchy up to the root node, we can interleave remainder blocks as much as possible. In the example of Figure 5, the two remainder blocks from setpoint Q 1 and setpoint Q 3 can eventually be interleaved by Rule 2 forming a single interleaved block. Once the final interleaved blocks are identified at the root node level, each interleaved block whose internal schedule is already determined is treated as an atomic schedule unit when it is scheduled with other interleaved block. Note that the total time for scheduling all 7 dwells released at every period p from τ 1 , τ 2 , τ 3 , τ 4 , τ 5 , τ 6 , and τ 7 is the time for maxI-interleaved blocks at the leaf node level, i.e., 12 ms, plus the time for scheduling all remainder blocks that is known at the root node level, i.e., 9 ms.

Until now, we explained interleaved-scheduling of dwells that come from the group of tasks using the same period option. When we schedule interleaved blocks from different period groups, we use EDF or RM scheduling algorithms by treating each interleaved block as an atomic schedule template, that is, non-preemptive block, to preserve the predetermined internal schedule of the interleaved block.

div.head: B. A scalable way to derive the schedulability envelope
div.p: Presuming the aforementioned radar dwell scheduling, this section describes a scalable way to derive the schedulability envelope, which can be used for QRAM in Eq. ( 5) in lieu of the schedulability check.

If a dwell J using setpoint Q s = (tx s , wa s , rx s , pw s ) is scheduled independently without being interleaved with others, the time for scheduling it is simply tx s + wa s + rx s . However, if J is interleaved with others, its contribution to the scheduling time is shorter than tx s + wa s + rx s . Thus, we need a better estimation of time for scheduling a single dwell J considering interleaving scenarios. Since our hierarchical interleaving tries to interleave up to maxI s same setpoint dwells at the leaf node level, maxI s is a good indicator for estimating a single dwell time. If maxI s dwells of setpoint Q s are interleaved together, the total time for scheduling maxI s dwells is tx s + wa s + maxI s • rx s as shown in Figure 6. Thus, the time for a single dwell of setpoint Q s can be approximately estimated as follows:
div.formula: e s = (tx s + wa s + maxI s • rx s ) maxI s . (13

div.p: One way to find the wcdev is to consider all remainder combinations (r 1 , r 2 , • • • , r K ) and simulate the hierarchical interleaving for each combination. Among them, by taking the one that makes the largest deviation, we can find wcdev. If maximum interleaving maxI of each setpoint is r, the remainder search space ranges from (0, 0, • • • , 0) to (r -1, r -1, • • • , r -1). Thus, the total number of remainder combinations is O(r K ) where K = N tx × N wa × N rx × N pw . Although this is a significant reduction of complexity compared to O(n K ) for searching entire solution space (note r << n and K << K), it is still problematic when the number of setpoints K is large.

To further reduce the search space, we use a hierarchical remainder search method by pruning non-worst-case remainder combinations as early as possible. To explain this, let us consider three setpoints in Figure 7. Supposed that maxI s for Q 1 , Q 2 , and Q 3 are 3, 2, and 2, respectively. Thus, there are three remainder cases at setpoint Q 1 (i.e., rem = 0, 1, 2), two cases at setpoint Q 2 (i.e., rem = 0, 1), and two cases at setpoint Q 3 (i.e., rem = 0, 1). Remember that the above naive remainder search method has to consider all 12(= 3 × 2 × 2) remainder combinations.

In the hierarchical remainder search, all remainder cases of a leaf node are combined with those of a sibling node at their parent node. div.head: IV. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
div.p: In this section, we compare the proposed schedulability envelope with the utilization bound check in Eq. ( 6) based on no-interleaved scheduling. For the comparison, we use 10 options in each domain of tx, wa, and pw assuming rx = tx. These options are summarized in the following table. The wa options correspond to 10 evenly quantized target ranges with the maximum coverage of 600 km. The tx and pw options are chosen based on the parameters reported in [6], [15]. When we make setpoints from the options of each domain, we consider the dependency among parameters. For example, a large wa is used for tracking a long range target that also requires reasonably long duration of tx and high power pw. Thus, a too short tx and a too low pw are not compatible with a large wa. Considering this dependency, a wa option with index i is assumed to be compatible with tx and pw options with index that ranges from i -2 to i + 2. Thus, one wa option is compatible with up to five surrounding options of tx and pw. Also, we use five harmonic period options 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms, 800 ms, and 1600 ms considering the temporal distance constraint as in [15], [14]. Therefore, the total number of setpoints is 1000. Note that the entire-space-search and naive-remainder-search have failed to derive the schedulability envelope for this large number of setpoints even after spending a long time, i.e., one month. The T DC threshold T DC th and energy threshold E th are 500 ms and 1400 J, respectively, over the exponential averaging time base of A = 1sec. Finally, we use maxBlock = 7ms to bound the blocking penalty.

For fair comparison of utilization bound check of Eq. ( 6) and the proposed schedulability envelope of Eq. ( 16), we 6) in a form of the schedulability envelope by normalizing the right hand side as 1.0. Thus, the resulting schedulability condition is

Now we can fairly compare the intercept ḃpi s of the nointerleave based utilization bound check in Eq. ( 17) with b pi s of the proposed envelope in Eq. ( 16). The larger the intercept of each setpoint is, the larger is the volume of envelope. This means the tighter estimation of resource consumption R(Q p s ) (i.e., inverse of the intercept) for each setpoint Q p s . As we can see in Figure 8, for most of setpoints, the intercepts of the proposed envelope are significantly larger than those of no-interleave based model. Among 1000 setpoints, for 880 setpoints, the proposed method has larger intercepts due to the advantage of interleaving. The maximum improvement is 69% and the average improvement is 55%. Only for 120 setpoints, the intercepts of the proposed envelope are slightly smaller. The setpoints for which the proposed envelope has smaller intercepts are the ones whose dwells cannot be interleaved at all, i.e., maxI = 1, due to high power and long transmit-time options. For those setpoints, we cannot take advantage of interleaving while we still have to pay the penalty of the worst case deviation wcdev. However, since the wcdev is small-less than one dwell length, the intercept decrease of the proposed envelope is less than 1% for all 120 setpoints.

To show the synergy gained from integrating QRAM and schedulability envelope from the perspective of system utility, we compare three different resource management policies; 1) the "Minimal setpoint" policy assumes no-interleaved scheduling and always assigns the minimal setpoint (i.e., minimal amount of resource) to each target, 2) the "QRAM with utilization bound" policy lets QRAM find the optimal resource assignment adapting to dynamic arrivals, departures, and movements of targets based on traditional no-interleave based utilization bound check, 3) the "QRAM with schedulability envelope" policy uses both QRAM and schedulability envelope to take advantage of interleaved scheduling in finding the optimal resource assignment adapting to dynamic target arrivals, departures, and movements. Figure 9 compares the system utility-total sum of task utility values, as increasing the average number of targets in the system. The utility of task τ i tracking target i is assumed to be given as a function of target importance w i and tracking error i (Q s ):
div.formula: V τi (Q s ) = w i 1 -e γ/ i(Qs )
div.p: where γ is a constant to map the tracking error to the utility value. We assume that the target importance, that is, the weight w i is given in proportional to target speed v i and reverseproportional to target distance r i . The tracking error i (Q s ) is given as a function of target state variables such as target distance r i and target speed v i , and operational parameters in Q s like radar transmission time tx s (= rx s ), radar transmission power pw s , and sampling period p s chosen from the values in Table II, based on the tracking error expressions in [5].

The "minimal-setpoint" policy always assigns the minimal setpoint even when the number of targets is very small and hence plenty of resource is available. This explains why the system utility linearly increases as the average target number increases. On the other hand, QRAM used in "QRAM with utilization bound" policy and "QRAM with schedulability envelope" policy tries to assign better setpoints to targets depending on resource availability. Thus, when the average target number is small, QRAM can assign better setpoints than minimal ones and thus achieve higher system utility than "minimal-setpoint" policy. When the average target number is small, no significant gap is observed between "QRAM with utilization bound" and "QRAM with schedulability envelope". This is because, in the under-saturated situation with only a few targets, both policies can assign the maximal setpoints to all tasks. However, as increasing the average number of targets, "QRAM with utilization bound" based on no-interleave assumption starts saturated first than "QRAM with schedulability envelope" that takes advantage of interleaving. Thus, we can observe a significant gap between the two policies as increasing the average target number. When the average number of targets is very large, "QRAM with utilization bound" converges to the "minimal setpoint" policy due to the limitation of utilization bound based on no-interleave scheduling assumption. On the other hand, the system utility by the "QRAM with the schedulability envelope" policy can increase even further since the schedulability envelope provides a larger volume of resource availability by taking advantage of interleaving.

V. CONCLUSION In this paper, we propose a novel framework for operating parameter assignment to concurrent multiple tasks in a phased array radar system with the objective of maximizing the system utility. The framework integrates existing resource management framework called QRAM with the notion of schedulability envelope.

For such framework, we propose a scalable way to derive the schedulability envelope for a large number of parameter options. The resulting schedulability envelope hides complex details of radar dwell scheduling and provides a linear abstraction for the schedulability check. The schedulability envelope is compatible with the resource constraint of QRAM. Thus, by integrating QRAM with the schedulability envelope, we can form a novel resource management (or parameter assignment) framework that works for a phased array antenna with complex physical characteristics.

Although the proposed schedulability envelope is scalable to a quite large number of QoS-setpoints, there is a limit. In the future, we will study the limit and develop QoS-parameter quantification to have a reasonable number of setpoints within the limit. We will also study the abstraction error due to the use of linear hyper-plane for the schedulability envelope. Eventually, we will form a generalized framework to handle many different types of complex resources.

Once we make all combinations, we apply the following two pruning conditions to minimize the number of combinations to be retained. Condition 1 -Drop a sufficiently-estimated block: For an interleaved block, if its actual time at is smaller than or equal to the estimated time et, i.e., negative or zero deviation, then the remainder deviation caused by this block cannot contribute to enlarge the worst case remainder deviation. Thus, we can safely drop such block. In Figure 7, the block in the rem=(2,1) case can be dropped since actual time at = 7 is already smaller than the estimated time et = 7.16. Once we drop the block from rem=(2,1) case, the case is subsumed by the rem=(0,0) case. Condition 2 -Drop a fully-interleaved block: For an interleaved block, if it is already fully interleaved meaning that no further interleaving is possible with any preferable block, its contribution to the worst case remainder deviation is fixed or committed. Thus, we can drop it after recording the committed deviation. In Figure 7, the block in the rem=(1,1) case cannot be interleaved with any possible block due to the energy and TDC constraints. Thus, it is already a fully interleaved block and hence it does not need to be considered for further interleaving. Thus, we can drop it after recording its deviation (atet = 6 -4.83 = 1.17) as committed one for the case. By dropping the block, the rem=(1,1) case is subsumed by rem=(0,0) case with the committed deviation of 1.17. This way, the subsuming remainder case can sufficiently represent the committed deviation of all subsumed remainder cases.

We repeat this combination and pruning up to the root level to find a sufficient estimation of worst case remainder deviation, i.e., wcdev used in Eq. (15). For each combination at the root level, its deviation is determined by adding the already committed deviation and the deviation of all blocks in the combination. Similarly, the deviation for the rem=(2,0,1) case is 0+1.34+1. The maximum deviation among all cases at the root node is a safe estimation of wcdev.
